newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM TO LOSE RENAULT JOBS DESPITE FIERCE BATTLE.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM TO LOSE RENAULT JOBS DESPITE FIERCE BATTLE.

text.p: The blow was effectively dealt in February, but it has taken over three months to sink in that French carmaker Renault is closing its Belgian plant costing at least 3,100 local jobs.

Pressure from politicians, mass rallies in Belgium and France, a public boycott, and even court victories have all failed to force a reversal of the closure decision inspired by the harsh realities of market economics.

Renault granted the plant in the Brussels suburb of Vilvoorde a stay of execution on Tuesday by commissioning an independent study to explore alternatives to the proposed closure of the assembly plant.
But Belgian unions did not hold out much hope, claiming Renault was trying to pull the wool over employees' eyes. Financial analysts also queried Renault's motives.
"The move is purely political, a show of good will for the electorate," a Belgian bank analyst said.
The offer was inspired by the newly-elected left-wing government in Paris, which has a 46 percent stake in the loss-making car-maker, he said.

Renault sounded the death-knell over the plant in Vilvoorde -- a small town of some 33,000 people -- on February 27, shocking not only its 3,100 staff and hundreds more at local supply firms, but the nation as a whole.
Citing a need to curb production locations in the face of tough competition and falling demand, Renault caught workers, and local and national politicians, off guard.
The backlash was instant and far angrier than the French giant had expected. Militant workers occupied the plant, holding millions of francs of finished cars hostage.
Hundreds of irate Renault workers marched on Brussels.
Arguments focused not only on keeping jobs in an economy with double-digit unemployment, but also on fending off allegations that Belgian labour costs were exorbitant.
Unions blamed the Brussels government, saying its drive to cut debt to qualify for Europe's single currency meant taxes and levies for social security could not be lowered.
After taxes and deductions for social security, Belgian net wages are between 45 and 60 percent of gross wages.
After Renault widened its restructuring plan to other European plants, protests spread.
Tens of thousands took to the streets, even months after Renault said Vilvoorde had to close, calling for an end to EMU-related austerity and a higher EU priority for jobs.
Politicians branded the decision unacceptable and called on the European Commission and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) to condemn it.
Their outcry reflected concern for the Renault jobs, the reputation of Belgium's highly qualified workforce and their future in the assembly sector and other product-finishing and processing areas.
Car makers Ford , Volvo , VW and Opel all have plants in Belgium and are major employers.
Renault did have some support from an unexpected quarter.

BASF Antwerpen NV, part of German chemicals group BASF AG, attacked regional and federal governments for failing to act on high labour costs and what it called unreasonable taxation. It said costs were more favourable in Spain and Great Britain.
Court victories in France and Belgium, where Renault was condemned for breaching plant closure procedure and inadequately consulting the workforce, briefly boosted morale in Vilvoorde.
The European Union backed the workers, but could offer little beyond vocal support and had to admit it could not stop cross-border decisions by multinational giants.

Vilvoorde workers grew battle-weary after months of occupying the plant and on occassion taking their protests to Renault in Paris and plants in France. Accepting the inevitable, some began looking for other jobs, found them, and left Renault.
